newsitem.title: USA: Study finds heart drug not prescribed for elderly.
newsitem.headline: Study finds heart drug not prescribed for elderly.

text.p: Beta-blockers, drugs used to prevent repeat heart attacks, are not being widely prescribed for elderly patients despite evidence they increase survival chances by 20 to 40 percent, a study said on Tuesday.

Misinformation and unsubstantiated concerns that the drugs can cause depression, fatigue and other side effects are probably behind the phenomenon, the report from Harvard Medical School and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care in Boston said.

The study covered 3,737 heart attack patients aged 65 and older who were on Medicare in New Jersey from 1987 to 1992. Only 21 percent of the group received beta-blocker therapy in the 90 days after they were discharged from the hospital following treatment for a heart attack, the report said.

The death rate among patients given beta-blockers was 43 percent less than for those who did not receive the drugs, said the study published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association.

The study said beta-blocker use after a heart attack has been shown to increase the chances of survival by from 20 to 40 percent. The drugs, in use since the 1960s, block specific sites on body tissues where chemicals are released from nerve endings, slowing the heart rate and reducing the force of contraction of the heart muscle.

The Agency for Health Care Policy and Research, which partially funded the research, said the study "is the first to demonstrate the survival benefits of long-term beta-blocker treatment in patients over age 75, a group that has been excluded from the clinical trials (for the drugs)."
